skill.name: instrument-app
skill.description: Add LogBrew error tracking and structured logging, then verify delivery by reading a test event.
skill.summary: Instrument an application with LogBrew and verify an event reaches the selected project.
skill.author: logbrewco

security_audit.summary: Most static matches are Markdown, SDK configuration, or safe secret-handling guidance. The Rails key export can expose a secret in shell history, and the workflow should validate install commands and review existing logs before forwarding them.

remediation.issue: The Rails example places a key in a shell command.
remediation.suggestion: Load the ingest key through a secret manager or protected environment configuration without typing it into shell history.

remediation.issue: The generated install command is executed without explicit validation.
remediation.suggestion: Validate the package manager, arguments, and package source, and request approval before running the command.

remediation.issue: Existing logs can be forwarded without a privacy review.
remediation.suggestion: Review existing log fields and SDK capture defaults, redact sensitive data, and obtain approval before enabling forwarding.

semantic_findings.description: The instructions execute the CLI-provided install command without requiring validation of its executable, arguments, or package source. A compromised CLI or manipulated output could cause unintended command execution.

semantic_findings.title: Existing logs may expose sensitive data
semantic_findings.description: Connecting the existing logger can send current logs to an external service without first checking their contents. Existing records may contain sensitive data despite the rules for newly added logs.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The skill forwards current logs while applying logging rules to added events; exposure depends on the existing application logs and SDK privacy settings.

content.value_statement: Application errors and logs can be difficult to trace across deployments. This skill configures LogBrew instrumentation and checks that a test event can be read back.
actual_capabilities: Detect the application runtime and framework using the LogBrew CLI.
Select SDK packages and provide setup examples for several frameworks.
Configure project ingest keys and service, environment, and release metadata.
Connect supported existing loggers and add a test event.
Read back events and check their service, environment, and release.
Apply guidance for structured logging, privacy, traces, and client shutdown.
limitations: Requires LogBrew access, appropriate credentials, and network connectivity for event delivery and read-back.
Frameworks without a full example require consulting the relevant SDK documentation.
A successful ingest response alone does not prove the event is readable.
Existing logs and SDK defaults require a privacy review before forwarding.

use_cases.title: Instrument a web service
use_cases.description: Add server-side error capture and structured logging to an existing service.

use_cases.title: Verify a deployment
use_cases.description: Send a test event and confirm its service, environment, and release.

use_cases.title: Improve logging practices
use_cases.description: Review event fields, secret handling, and trace correlation guidance.

prompt_templates.title: Review the application
prompt_templates.prompt: Identify the framework, existing logger, and entry point in this application.

prompt_templates.title: Add instrumentation
prompt_templates.prompt: Set up LogBrew for this application using its existing framework and secret configuration.

prompt_templates.title: Verify delivery
prompt_templates.prompt: Send a safe test event and verify its service, environment, and release by reading it back.

prompt_templates.title: Review an existing integration
prompt_templates.prompt: Inspect the existing instrumentation for duplicate senders, sensitive log fields, release metadata, and shutdown flushing.

output_examples.input: Instrument an Express service and verify delivery.
output_examples.output: The service uses the Express integration. The test event was read back with the expected service, environment, and release.

output_examples.input: Check why a test event is missing.
output_examples.output: The read-back returned no event. Check the project, time range, ingest key, and client flush behavior before reporting success.

best_practices: Store ingest keys in protected secret configuration and never paste them into chat.
Review existing logs and SDK capture defaults for sensitive data before forwarding.
Confirm the test event through read-back and verify its deployment metadata.
anti_patterns: Treat an accepted send as proof that an event is readable.
Add a second sender for the same signal without discussing existing instrumentation.
Log credentials, full request bodies, or unnecessary personal data.

faq.question: What does this skill set up?
faq.answer: It guides LogBrew SDK installation, application instrumentation, and test event verification.

faq.question: Which frameworks are covered?
faq.answer: The references list many runtimes and include examples for Express, Next.js, React, FastAPI, Django, Flask, Gin, Rails, and ASP.NET Core.

faq.question: Does it need a LogBrew account?
faq.answer: The workflow requires access to a LogBrew project and appropriate ingest and read credentials.

faq.question: Should I paste an API key into chat?
faq.answer: No. Use protected secret configuration or an owner-only key file.

faq.question: Does a successful send prove setup is complete?
faq.answer: No. Read the event back and check the service, environment, and release.

faq.question: Does this automatically make existing logs private?
faq.answer: No. Review existing logs, SDK settings, and redaction before forwarding data.
